title: Russian Federation
capsule: The Russian Federation emerged in December 1991 as the principal successor state to the Soviet Union after its formal dissolution, inheriting the USSR's nuclear arsenal, UN Security Council seat, and the bulk of its territory — 17.1 million square kilometres spanning eleven time zones. Under Boris Yeltsin (1991–1999) the state navigated a painful transition to a market economy, the First Chechen War (1994–1996), and constitutional crisis; Vladimir Putin's accession in 2000 marked a reassertion of centralized authority and a decade of oil-fuelled economic expansion. The federation's geopolitical posture hardened progressively: the 2008 war with Georgia, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine produced sweeping Western sanctions and reshaped its international standing through 2024.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial extent is precisely attested by modern administrative and international boundary datasets; the principal uncertainty concerns de facto versus de jure control in contested areas (Crimea from 2014, parts of eastern Ukraine from 2022).
